Economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos was announced after a meeting of eurozone leaders.
The president of the European Council says eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the new European Central Bank (ECB) president.
Antonio Costa also announced that Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier have been recommended as members of the ECB executive board, and noted that this paves the way for the formal appointment of the new European Central Bank leadership by December’s European Union summit.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the first Spaniard to take the role, and succeeds France’s Christine Lagarde at the Frankfurt-based institution at a challenging time for the eurozone.
Currently head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Basel-based forum for the world’s major central banks, the 55-year-old will take over in February, when Lagarde would step down several months before her term expires in October next year.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post. The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.
Diplomats have described the Spanish economist as a “steady hand” to steer the institution, with a reputation for pragmatism and consensus-building.
As the Bank of Spain’s chief economist and later governor, he navigated the aftermath of Spain’s 2010s banking crisis, years of ultra-low inflation, COVID-19 and the 2022 inflation surge that followed the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
He also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for banks.
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.
He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second-most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.

Ford enters the World Endurance Championship in 2027 with the new prototype.
Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win . Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy , and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.
“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It’s the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”
Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.
The hybrid system and transmission are also standard parts. But Ford supplies the engine—a 5.4 L V8 based on the Mustang’s Coyote engine—as well as software to control the hybrid powertrain. A non-hybridized version of the Coyote has already been racing effectively under the hood of the Ford Mustang GT3.
The technical regulations also allow for more styling freedom than we often see in racing. The absolute amount of aerodynamic downforce is capped, as is the minimum drag, so OEMs are encouraged to use road car styling details to create a closer link between prototype and road car. I’ll probably need to spend more time looking at it to spot those road car cues, but I do see quite a few superficial similarities with the Genesis LMDh car, as well as the Ferrari Hypercar .
Despite being an American car brand, Ford doesn’t have plans as yet to enter IMSA’s WeatherTech championship, so don’t expect to see the GT41 next January racing at Daytona. Instead, it will take its first green flag in Qatar in March, the first of WEC’s nine races next season.
Ford should find it an extremely competitive championship. Although Peugeot and Alpine will not race next year, McLaren is also entering, alongside returning teams from Aston Martin, BMW, Cadillac, Genesis, Ferrari, and Toyota, which this year won Le Mans and the overall title, following three years of Ferrari domination.

The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.
Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline . It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia want to opt out of €45bn Ukraine loan, as Germany tries to protect funding from possible far-right French presidency
EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.
Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz , reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.
Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds.
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia, net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin , has accused Merz of blackmail.
Separately, Germany is seeking to insulate future EU funding for Ukraine from a Marine Le Pen victory in next year’s French presidential elections. The far-right National Rally leader, who is leading in opinion polls, has vowed to stop French financial aid for Ukraine. Berlin wants to ensure future decisions on funding Kyiv via the EU budget are made by a majority of EU member states, rather than unanimously. The current system requires consensus, enabling one country to veto a decision.
In a more hopeful sign for Kyiv, Bulgaria, which had been against the loan, said on Thursday it was ready to contribute as long as its share was not linked to weapons.
“Bulgaria is going to ‌take part in the loan of 20bn [for] non-military support ​for Ukraine,” the country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said as he arrived at the summit. “We have a ⁠huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living ​in Ukraine. Our wish is ​to concentrate our support ​in that ‌area. We are ​going ​to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons.”
The European Commission last week proposed a €45bn EU loan for Ukraine to fill a funding hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks. EU officials proposed €25bn for military spending and €20bn for Ukraine’s civilian needs, such as schools and hospitals.
Arriving at the summit, Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, was in no mood for compromise. “Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and [the] Czech Republic. We will fight for this money,” he said, referring to the EU’s cohesion funds, which are intended to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.
Babiš said his country needed a highway to Austria and more hospitals. “Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately. And the most important is the life of our citizens,” he said, adding that the EU should “do everything” to support peace in Ukraine.
But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said: “It’s not acceptable to simply kidnap the support for Ukraine by saying that we will accept the European Union support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves. That is not a reasonable way of thinking.”
However, some governments that support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down.
The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034.
EU leaders are discussing a €1.78tn proposal presented by the European Council president, António Costa, last Saturday, which represents a 10% reduction on the original €2tn plan from the European Commission.
EU officials want to finalise a budget deal by the end of the year before a sequence of big elections in 2027 complicates finding an agreement, with most concern over French presidential elections in the spring. As well as ceasing funding for Ukraine, Le Pen has vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, who is battling to preserve EU farm subsidies for French farmers and a larger budget, has also indicated he could walk away from talks if there was no deal by the end of the year. “An agreement is not an end in itself, nor an objective in itself if it were based on unbalanced foundations,” an Élysée source said before the summit. If the elements are not right, “the president thinks it will not be possible for him to continue this discussion beyond December”, the source said.
The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said it was important to get a budget agreement before the end of the year as “the prospects of doing it in the first half of 2027 are very dim”.
Others have pushed back against allowing French elections to dominate the EU budget timetable, and have said making Le Pen the focus gives her ammunition to make a case that the EU is against her political movement. “We should be aware of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” said one senior EU diplomat. “Let’s not be paralysed by elections happening in six months.”
Costa, arriving at the summit on Thursday, said all leaders needed to approach discussions with an “open mind, a constructive approach and a sense of compromise” as he called for the budget to be approved in a “timely” way, adding: “That means by the end of this year.”
The budget has to be agreed unanimously, but countries are deeply split. In one camp are the so-called frugals – net contributors to the EU budget such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden – which want to reduce the overall size and shift spending priorities to defence and competitiveness, rather than farm subsidies and regional funds.
In the other camp are 17 countries in southern, central and eastern Europe, which want to ensure the flow of EU funds to traditional policies and oppose cuts.
France sits in neither camp, but has vowed to protect the common agriculture policy (CAP), which benefits French farmers. Maintaining farm payments would make it harder for Le Pen to unravel the budget. On the eve of the summit, Macron said “not a single euro of the CAP must be withheld from France in the next European multi-annual budget”.
Le Pen welcomed press reports that Paris was pushing for increased agriculture spending, but said Macron’s position had “nothing to do” with defending French farmers. “The objective would be to dissuade us – if the French entrusted us with the responsibility to govern – from defending French interests in European budgetary negotiations” she wrote on X.

Spanish monetary economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos on Thursday was set to replace France's Christine Lagarde as the new head of the European Central Bank (ECB). His nomination comes as the Europe's most powerful financial institution grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and a cost of living crisis.
European leaders on Thursday chose the former head of Spain ’s central bank, Pablo Hernandez de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank ( ECB ) as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the Eurozone .
Agreement on the three posts was reached at a summit in Brussels, said an EU diplomat tasked with communicating for the Irish Presidency and speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to be named. French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed the result on X.
De Cos's nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.
The former Spanish central bank governor and the current general manager of the Bank for International Settlements will take over when current chief Lagarde steps down ‌early on February 7.
Read more ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down in February 2027, nine months before term ends
The way for him to replace her as the next ECB chief became clear on ⁠Thursday after the Netherlands decided to back him, effectively standing down its own candidate Klaas Knot.
The reshuffle comes as the ECB grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and worries that political turmoil in France could trigger broader financial market ​stress affecting other Eurozone countries.
De Cos's appointment hands the top job to a southern European policymaker and ally ‌of former ECB President Mario Draghi , reinforcing expectations that the central bank would ultimately use its firepower to contain any new sovereign debt crisis.
De Cos, 55, a trained monetary economist, has built a reputation for independent thinking anchored in economic theory, and pragmatism picked up over a decade served in policymaking roles.
He worked in various staff positions at ​the ECB and the Bank of Spain early in his career before making a rare jump to the policymaking level as governor of ​the national central bank, serving on the ECB's rate-setting Governing Council.
De Cos is a veteran ​of crises including Spain's banking sector bailout , the COVID-19 pandemic, and the post-pandemic inflation surge that forced the ECB into its fastest interest rate-hiking cycle on record.
While southern European policymakers are often considered "doves" favouring easier ​monetary policy, colleagues and ECB watchers say De Cos is pragmatic and a moderate who cannot be boxed into any such category.
ECB policy is decided by the 27-member Governing Council, meaning even the president has limited scope to steer interest rates single-handedly.
In any case, any dovish bias would only be relevant if inflation was slightly above target, and this year's surge in price pressures would force any ECB president to keep raising interest rates .
At 4 percent, ⁠inflation is now twice the central bank's target and policymakers speaking on and off the record appear unanimous that a rate hike in December is inevitable.
The path beyond ⁠is murky, however. Markets expect ​just one more upward move, given the recent retreat in oil prices and an expected decline in inflation from the spring, when statistical base effects start knocking year-earlier figures from the data set.

The bloc is holding an extraordinary summit in Brussels to discuss its budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 as well as a new loan for Ukraine.
European Union leaders are struggling to reach a deal on the bloc’s nearly $1.76 trillion budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 and agree a new $49bn loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.
The differences were visible at an extraordinary EU summit in Brussels on Thursday, where some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget.
Most, however, wanted extra funds for important new priorities and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.
“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time, there is a series of tasks we must fulfil reliably.”
“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defence,” he told reporters.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Hungary’s Prime Minister Peter Magyar were more forthright.
“We’re light-years away from a solution,” Meloni told reporters before the summit. “We are not willing to sign off on a budget under which we would have to give more to receive less,” she added.
“Hearing the completely opposing positions in the room, the chance of an agreement today is virtually zero, but a Christmas agreement does not seem likely either,” Magyar posted on Facebook.
The new joint spending package is small compared with national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. But it does require unanimous approval from all member states.
While the budget only starts in 2028, leaders want to have a deal by year-end because there are elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia that could complicate negotiations.
“The budget needs to be modernised and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”
European Council President Antonio Costa, who is chairing the summit that could run into Friday, called on the leaders to approach the debate with an “open mind, a constructive approach and the sense of compromise”.
He said that an agreement is needed “by the end of this year and for this we need to reach unanimity”.
Ukraine is a big part of the EU’s budget puzzle. The spending package foresees $110bn for the government in Kyiv over seven years. The leaders must also decide on the new loan and whether the costs of servicing it should be drawn from the budget.
Earlier this month, Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if no “collective commitment” was made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception”.
Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. Merz repeated his warning on Thursday and said that “we will talk about this in depth in one-on-one talks”.
“We must ensure that Ukraine receives sufficient support in the coming years,” Merz said as he entered the summit. “I don’t think anyone in Europe can have any interest in seeing new waves of refugees from Ukraine if this war does not come to an end.”
Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of $99bn to cover most of the Ukrainian government’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.
As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.
The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.
Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc…
… and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model , on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.
In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.
Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.
That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.
Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts . It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.
If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.
podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1
This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:
My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.
I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet.
On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:
Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.
* It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp

Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.
While revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, Trump has tried time and again to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is underway in the US.
The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), an agency within the US Department of Commerce, calculates gross domestic product, or GDP, numbers.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.
Trump has repeatedly claimed since taking office in January 2025 that an economic “golden age” is taking hold on his watch. Many Americans have been grappling with a higher cost of living, however – exacerbated by the economic fallout of his war on Iran – and backed Democrats in the midterms.
Trump continued his acerbic well-wishing for “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.
And he revisited another ongoing beef with the news media over his controversial focus on White House renovations and decorations. “I want to commiserate with those reporters and citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House.”

Democratic senator Chuck Schumer, vying to be majority leader in the chamber following his party’s victories in this month’s election took a more conventional approach , wishing “everyone in New York and across America a joyous and restful Thanksgiving holiday with your friends and family”.

United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation.
Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.
The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3 percent from the advance estimate of 3.4 percent it announced on October 29. Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 elections.
“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE,” Trump said in a Truth Social post without providing evidence for the accusation.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” he said.
Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fail to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. Gross domestic product (GDP) figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a prescheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.
The BEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has previously said GDP estimates can differ from the final numbers because advance estimates for quarterly growth lack complete source data on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services.
A May article coauthored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that for GDP, the estimates released 90 days after initial estimates typically differed by 0.52 percentage points throughout this century.
“That is, over these 25 years, more complete source data expanded or contracted BEA’s estimates of real GDP growth on average by about half a percentage point per quarter,” wrote Arora and coauthor Rebecca Pocase.
Last year, Trump fired a top Department of Labor official after a weak jobs report, accusing her without evidence of manipulating the figures, a move that added to already growing concerns about the quality of economic data published by the federal government.

⁠Sputnik-S, a nuclear-enabled satellite, has been assembled by Russia and could be launched in 60 days, reports say
Russia is reportedly preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space later this year, in a scenario that could pose a significant threat to global communications.
German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.
A report by the German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said western intelligence services, including Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces, had exchanged information showing that a nuclear-enabled satellite, named ⁠Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in ⁠the Moscow region. It could be launched this year. A German government spokesperson said it was taking the intelligence reports “very seriously”.
In space, where there is no atmosphere, there is no mushroom cloud. Instead, the energy from a nuclear explosion is released as radiation. A detonation would be particularly damaging in low Earth orbit, or up to 1,200 miles above Earth, where most satellites operate.
Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in the UK, said the main effects were twofold: everything within line of sight of the detonation could be zapped by X-rays and other forms of radiation which could knock out or damage satellites within thousands of miles; secondly, radiation particles could be emitted into the lower atmosphere and form a new “Van Allen belt”, the term for two belts of radiation that circle the Earth and shield it from the impact of solar storms.
It would be a replay of an event in 1962 when the US detonated a thermonuclear bomb 250 miles above Earth’s surface – in low Earth orbit – in an event called Starfish Prime. There were many fewer satellites then but it shortened the life of two craft: the Telstar 1 and Ariel-1 satellites.
“Starfish caused severe radiation over a period of months to at least half the satellites then working on orbit, which was not very many at that point,” said McDowell.
Keith Ryden, a professor of space engineering at the University of Surrey in the UK, said low Earth orbit satellites were vulnerable to bursts of radiation.
“Since natural levels of radiation are relatively low in this region, satellites located there are not designed for high radiation levels so they would be vulnerable to unexpected increases,” he says.
There are about 17,000 satellites in lower Earth orbit, including satellites important to weather forecasting, climate monitoring and the military as well as Elon Musk’s network of satellites that form the Starlink broadband network. The latter is crucial to assisting Ukraine’s efforts in repelling the invasion of Russia.
The International Space Station, in which Russia is a partner, is also in low Earth orbit. Musk’s proposed constellation of space datacentres would operate there as well.
Satellites handling TV broadcast, GPS and other communications are in higher orbits that are less easy for a nuclear weapon to affect.
McDowell said the artificial Van Allen belt caused by Starfish Prime was around for five years.
“There will be immediate impacts from a detonation but there are lasting environmental effects that will damage satellites in the longer run. It could take several years, up to a decade, for the trapped particles to diffuse out of the radiation belt,” he said.
Ryden added: “Just as important, the space industry would not have the capacity to rebuild and launch the required number of spacecraft in a short time.”
Hundreds of miles below the Starfish Prime explosion, streetlights in Hawaii were knocked out, burglar alarms were set off in the area, and phone calls were disrupted.
“There might be an impact on computers and electronic systems in the region of earth where the explosion is visible,” said McDowell.
Ryden added that Starfish and other nuclear tests took place over sparsely populated areas so the location of the detonation was key.
“It does depend a lot on where the detonation happens,” he said.
Starfish Prime also created stunning aurora effects as the sky was lit up in shades of green, yellow, red and, according to one report, “tremendous white rainbows”.
“There would be huge auroral effects. It would not be a subtle thing. It’s hard to be subtle with nukes,” said McDowell.
A European security official told the Guardian that they were doubtful that Russia would detonate a nuclear device in space. They said it could cause significant damage to western economies, but that it stood to significantly harm Russia as well. Such an explosion would be hard to control and would probably damage Russia’s own satellites, as well as, potentially, China’s. “It would be shooting themselves in the leg,” they said.
They pointed at Russia’s nuclear blackmail earlier in its war in Ukraine, including when Russia put its nuclear forces on high alert in 2022, followed by movements of troops and weapons. “They were bluffing then – and this looks like a bluff now,” said the official. McDowell said he was sceptical about Russia detonating a nuclear weapon in space, because it was “such a stupid idea” to commit what would be viewed as an act of war.

Gérard Depardieu has faced a series of allegations in recent years on film sets and elsewhere
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.
Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".
Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.
But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc ( call out your pig).
Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.
Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

“Regarding the targeting of a vital site in the country as a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, the two injured Italian nationals have died as a result of their injuries,” said Kuwait’s Defence Ministry. It had earlier said the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified “material damage”.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said the Iranian drone attack happened while the Kuwaiti National Guard and Kuwaiti military were meeting with an Italian delegation that was visiting, including the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, as well as the Italian ambassador to Kuwait.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was informed of the “tragic deaths”.
“On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims’ families,” Meloni wrote on X.
The countries of the Gulf region “have in one voice said an attack against one is an attack against all and have continued to condemn these attacks as a violation of sovereignty”, but we’ve seen an uptick in attacks since September, said Basravi, reporting from Doha.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned Thursday’s “brutal” attack.
In a statement, Albudaiwi stressed that Iran’s continued attacks on Kuwait, targeting its vital facilities and endangering the lives of civilians, constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.
There was no immediate comment from Iran regarding the attack.
But it was in line with Tehran’s “policy change”, said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from the Iranian capital.
“Increasingly we have heard from the Iranian officials … saying that this state of no war, no peace cannot remain in place forever, and Iran is working on some military options … to break the status quo,” said Serdar.
The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the strait.
Thursday’s deadly attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences to counter drone strikes launched by Iran – the first since early September.

Watch: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait was targeted by Iran, Italian and Kuwaiti authorities said
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".
Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.
Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.
The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.
In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.
The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder
It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.
Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.
About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kgs of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.
Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.
The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.
Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China, and a fireworks display.
Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.
Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing.
In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.
India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.

Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people .
The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.
The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.
In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.
The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.
Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.
The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.
The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.
By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.
“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”
A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.
“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”
The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.
The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.
“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.
Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.
The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.
Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.
Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.
“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.
Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.
Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

Labour is jubilant it has got numbers down to levels the Tories could not but it was helped by factors beyond its control
Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic
David Cameron was the leader of the opposition when he made a comment on overall migration that was used to interrogate every Tory leader for the next 14 years.
Asked in January 2010 on the BBC by the interviewer Andrew Marr to address comments made by the archbishop of Canterbury calling for the population to remain under 70 million, Cameron said net immigration levels of 200,000 a year were “too much”.
“We would like to see net immigration in the tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands,” he said.
It became a full-blown promise in Cameron’s Tory manifesto that year; and it was there again when he won the 2015 general election, alongside a promise to hold an EU referendum. And the promise was repeated by Theresa May in 2017 as she narrowly defeated the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.
Both Tory leaders struggled with the actual net migration numbers, which fluctuated between 195,000 and 303,000.
Boris Johnson was pressed on whether he would revive Cameron’s pledge, and his 2019 manifesto said “overall numbers will come down”. Rishi Sunak, five years later, said he would like to see the figures get to tens of thousands but his manifesto promised that “numbers would fall every year”.
It has led to some crowing by Labour – and frustration from the Tories – that numbers have finally dipped below six figures under the current government.
Migration analysts said the Tories struggled throughout the 2010s because the UK was a full member of the EU and had no way of controlling inward EU migration.
EU citizens made up a majority of immigration and net migration in the run-up to the 2016 EU referendum. Since 2022, however, EU net migration has been negative.
As the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic, Johnson opened the doors to non-EU migration and to Ukrainians and people from Hong Kong.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “The previous government introduced some relatively liberal policies, including visa schemes for care workers, mid-skilled workers, Ukrainians and Hongkongers, and post-study work visas for international students.”
Several conditions that enabled Labour to achieve net migration of below 100,000 did not exist for most of the time that the Tories were in power, Sumption said.
First, the UK was part of the EU for most of the Tories’ time in office and so it had little control over inward EU migration.
Second, the Office for National Statistics still relied on an older methodology for estimating migration of British citizens under the Conservatives . The new method, introduced last year, has taken “tens of thousands off the net migration figure”, she said.
Third, high migration under the previous government – and particularly under Johnson – has left a temporary legacy of high numbers of non-EU citizens leaving the UK under Labour.
“Non-EU emigration is around 130,000 higher than it was for most of the 2010s, and that is only possible because so many non-EU citizens arrived a few years ago,” she said.
The Tories throughout the 2010s were also under pressure from business and their own party to ensure that they could expand the economy and offer tax cuts, a former cabinet minister said.
“Migration was an issue then but not top of the agenda as it has been for the last few years,” they said.
The Tories claimed credit for the fall on Thursday, after introducing immigration restrictions in the last parliament. But Labour insisted it had been the one to “restore control” at the borders after net migration came close to 1 million under the Tories.
Sumption said the net migration figure could fall further but may also be expected to rise again.
“The lower figures we see today are partly a result of government policy but partly the result of methodological changes and an increase in emigration that is expected to be temporary. The numbers could still have further to fall but there is no reason to assume they will remain below 100,000 ffor ever, even if policy remains the same,” she said.

Latest figures show difference between number of people arriving and leaving UK was ⁠77,000 in ​year ‌to ‌June
Analysis: How much of the fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?
Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was ⁠77,000 in ⁠the ​year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.
The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from an estimated 171,000 in 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.
UK net migration is also for the first time in the “tens of thousands” since that target was set but never fulfilled by David Cameron’s government in 2010. An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the data published on Thursday.
The 62% fall over the past 12 months – from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 – results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen more than 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.
Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, bring family members to the UK or apply for asylum.
Keir Starmer’s policies last year made care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspended family reunion for refugees and toughened restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.
Emigration remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared with the year ending June 2025.
Most people leaving the UK to live in another country were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including those who moved to the UK as part of the “Boriswave” from 2021 onwards when immigration was unusually high.
Reacting to the figures, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said Labour’s policies should be credited for the drop. It will be seen as a boost to Andy Burnham’s plans to keep hold of “red wall” seats in any future general election.
“The Conservatives lost control of our borders. Year upon year, they promised they would bring net migration down to the tens of thousands. Instead, they let it reach close to a million a year, overseeing four decades worth of migration in their last four years alone.
“This government has restored control. Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people,” she said.
Burnham said of the figures: “I think we are finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see.”
Asked about the UK’s future relationship with the EU and whether freedom of movement should be up for discussion, he said the Channel crossings crisis “arose significantly in the post-Brexit years when we lost that ability to collaborate with our European partners, and we’ve had to work hard to catch up again … So, no, I don’t think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country.”
The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.
Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.
The end of social care visas has caused numbers to fall from 108,000 at their peak to just 1,400 last year.
Migration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.
Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.
The Conservatives claimed their policies under Rishi Sunak’s administration were responsible for the drop, including restrictions on family members that could be brought over by care workers and changes stopping dependants moving to the UK with international students.
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.”
Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said net migration could drop even further next year, and may have a “fiscal cost”.
“We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall.
“Falling net migration is not automatically a problem for the UK economy, especially in the long run. Falling asylum migration is expected to benefit public finances. On the other hand, the number of migrants on skilled work visas has fallen even more over the past year, and that is expected to have a fiscal cost,” he said.
Sunder Katwala, the director of the British Future thinktank, said the figures “will come as a surprise to most of the public” who still tended to believe that immigration was rising. “It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next,” he said.
Other data published by the Home Office showed the number of asylum seekers living in hotels was at the lowest level since records began in 2022, but there was a 9% rise of those in “dispersal” accommodation – privately managed houses, flats or rooms in properties of multiple occupancy. There has been a drop in the number of new asylum applicants and Channel crossings are down 39% year on year, with 23,983 people having arrived in the UK in small boats in 2026.

There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.
The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.
Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.
The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.
It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.
The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".
The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".
Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."
The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.
It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.
The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.
Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.
This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?
The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

Football’s governing body says hackers accessed a limited set of personal and business data
Fifa confirmed that hackers gained access to a “limited set of personal and business information” in a cyber-attack, amid heightened concern over digital vulnerabilities of leading organizations and institutions.
The global soccer governing body said it “condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data”, in a statement to the Associated Press on Thursday. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were Fifa files. The post has since then been removed after the account was suspended from X.
The Fifa cyber-attack is the latest high-profile digital disruption to hit a major organization in recent weeks.
Microsoft experienced a widespread outage earlier this month that caused disruption to millions of users, organizations and businesses across the globe. The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents.
The following day, the US experienced an unprecedented nationwide disruption to air travel that prompted a “ground stop” order to be issued by the US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration, which cited “communication issues” impacting air traffic control centers.
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, later said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
Three days later, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Such disruptions have intensified fear and concerns about the advancement of artificial intelligence, and the potential risks, even though there is no direct evidence that AI directly sparked the issues.
ESPN reported that unnamed sources said the Fifa hack accounted for less than 0.1% of data held by the organization, an that the breach was not a result of systems or technology failure on Fifa’s part, with hackers said to hav e gained access by impersonating staff.
As of now, it has not been shared when the cyber-attack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.
“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said its statement sent to the Associated Press.
The cyber-attack comes as Gianni Infantino, Fifa’s president, is under scrutiny for a proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino admitted the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.
The plan has caused tensions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved.
Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term.
